{'paper_id': 'ma-rlhf', 'title': 'MA-RLHF: REINFORCEMENT LEARNING FROM HU-MAN FEEDBACK WITH MACRO ACTIONS', 'abstract': '{chaiyekun,fanghuang,wangshuohuan}@baidu.com sunhaoran0402@gmail.com', 'pdf_parse': {'paper_id': 'ma-rlhf', 'abstract': [{'text': '{chaiyekun,fanghuang,wangshuohuan}@baidu.com sunhaoran0402@gmail.com', 'section': 'Abstract', 'sec_num': None}], 'body_text': [{'text': 'Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized natural language processing tasks, demonstrating impressive capabilities across a wide range of applications such as code generation (Roziere et al., 2023; Chai et al., 2023; Lozhkov et al., 2024), mathematical reasoning (Lewkowycz et al., 2022; Anil et al., 2023), and dialogue assistance (OpenAI, 2023; Team et al., 2023; Anthropic). Despite these successes, aligning LLMs with human values and preferences remains a critical challenge. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has emerged as a promising approach to address this alignment issue by incorporating human evaluations into the training process (Christiano et al., 2017; Ziegler et al., 2019; Stiennon et al., 2020). Existing RLHF (Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022; Askell et al., 2021) methods mainly optimize decisions at the level of individual tokens, and require to process a vast number of minute adjustments. However, this fine-grained training paradigm can lead to the credit assignment problem (Kaelbling et al., 1996; Pang et al., 2019; Machado et al., 2023b; Pignatelli et al., 2023), particularly when dealing with long-distance dependencies. As LLM agents attempt to optimize decisions across extensive sequences, the difficulty in attributing the credits of actions to specific tokens complicates the reinforcement learning (RL) process (Pignatelli et al., 2024). Moreover, the use of subword tokenization, such as Byte-Pair Encoding (Sennrich et al., 2016), often splits words into smaller pieces. For instance, OpenAI’s ChatGPT1 treats each token as three quarters of a word on average, resulting in sequences that are 33 \\% longer than word counts (OpenAI, 2024) and further exacerbates the credit assignment problem. Additionally, standard RLHF methods may overlook essential local co-occurrence patterns or inherent structures between adjacent tokens in natural language. For example, consider the phrase Big \\mathtt { A p p l e } ^ { 2 } , treating \\mathtt { B i g } and \\mathtt { A p p l e } as isolated decisions misses the cohesive meaning of the term, which actually refers to the “New York City”. The token-level granularity of natural language can hinder the agent’s ability to capture high-level language constructs in RL optimization, as some sequences are better understood when evaluated holistically. To address these challenges, we propose a new framework called macro-action RLHF (MA-RLHF) that incorporate macro action — sequences of tokens or high-level language constructs — into the RLHF framework. The concept of macro actions, has been explored in the literature of planning (Iba, 1989; Korf, 1985; Sacerdoti, 1974) and reinforcement learning (Thrun & Schwartz, 1994; Precup et al., 1997; Hauskrecht et al., 2013), simplifies decision-making by operating at high levels of temporal abstraction under the framework of semi-Markov Decision Processes (SMDPs) (Sutton et al., 1999b). Macro actions leverage temporal abstraction by chunking the sequences and reducing the decision resolution, enabling the agent to learn from “long-sighted” macro-level actions instead of “short-sighted” token-level actions. This can potentially lead to improved learning efficiency and scalability. Alternatively, MA-RLHF can also be interpreted from the perspective of reversing tokenization; MA-RLHF serves as a de-tokenization process to reconstruct high-level language units from subword pieces. By merging tokens into macro actions, we reduce the number of decision points and shorten decision trajectories, alleviating the credit assignment problem caused by long temporal distances. To conclude, our main contributions are as follows: • We propose MA-RLHF, a simple yet effective RLHF framework that integrates the macro actions into RLHF to align LLMs with human preference. In the context of RLHF, we denote the state s _ { t } = \\{ s _ { 0 } , a _ { 0 } , a _ { 1 } , . . . , a _ { t - 1 } \\} as the sequence of tokens generated up to time step t , while s _ { 0 } represents the initial states, i.e., the prompt, and a _ { t } represents the token selected at the t { \\cdot } -th position.', 'section': 'RLHF FOR HUMAN ALIGNMENT', 'sec_num': '2.2'}, {'text': 'Macro actions, also referred to as options (Sutton et al., 1999b), are high-level constructs that encapsulate a sequence of primitive actions (i.e., subword tokens); by its definition, macro actions allows an agent to operate at a coarser temporal scale. In the context of LLMs, a macro action \\omega _ { \\tau } consists of a sequence of consecutive tokens, i.e., \\omega _ { \\tau } = \\{ a _ { t _ { \\tau } } , a _ { t _ { \\tau } + 1 } , \\ldots , a _ { t _ { \\tau + 1 } - 1 } \\} , where t _ { \\tau } is the starting index of the \\tau { \\cdot } -th macro action. In the context of LLMs, expanding the action space with additional macro actions/tokens results in re-architecting the LLM’s vocabulary and retraining the model, which is computationally prohibitive. In our implementation, we apply the identical action / vocabulary space as pretrained LLMs, considering the fact that defining macro actions as one options (e.g., one macro action per n -gram) would require re-architecting the LLM’s vocabulary and retraining the model, which is computationally infeasible. Meanwhile, our macro action termination methods are rule-based, including linguistics- or perplexity-driven approaches; future research could explore more complex or learnable termination strategies to further enhance performance. Furthermore, regarding the generalization of MA-RLHF, our experiments are conducted using models with up to 27B parameters; exploring more advanced models, such as LLaMA 3.1 405B (Dubey et al., 2024) or other state-of-the-art architectures and tasks (e.g., mathematical and complex reasoning), may provide additional insights into the scalability of MA-RLHF. Lastly, although we observe significant improvements in training efficiency, further investigation into the trade-offs between training stability and performance under diverse real-world conditions is necessary. Addressing these limitations will pave the way for more robust applications of MA-RLHF. # B EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS # B.1 DATASETS AND TASKS TL;DR Summarization In this task, the policy is asked to generate summarizations for Reddit posts. ## Overview of the plan
# MA-RLHF Reproduction Plan

## Overview

MA-RLHF introduces macro actions into the standard RLHF/PPO pipeline. The core idea is simple: instead of computing advantages and policy gradients at the individual token level, tokens are grouped into "macro actions" (chunks), and the PPO objective is applied at that coarser granularity. The policy architecture itself is unchanged — only the credit assignment and optimization steps differ.

---

## 1. System Architecture

The full pipeline has three sequential stages, each building on the previous:

```
Pre-trained LM → SFT Model → Reward Model → MA-PPO Policy
```

Four model roles exist simultaneously during PPO training:
- **Policy model** (πθ): the model being trained
- **Reference model** (πsft): frozen SFT model for KL penalty
- **Critic model** (Vπ): value function, initialized from reward model
- **Reward model** (rφ): frozen, provides scalar reward

---

## 2. Methodology Details

### 2.1 Macro Action Formalization

A macro action ωτ is a contiguous sequence of tokens:
```
ωτ = {a_{t_τ}, a_{t_τ+1}, ..., a_{t_{τ+1}-1}}
```

The joint probability of a macro action is the product of individual token probabilities:
```
π_θ(ωτ | sτ) = ∏_{t=t_τ}^{t_{τ+1}} π_θ(a_t | a_{<t})
```

In log space (which is what we actually compute):
```
log π_θ(ωτ | sτ) = Σ_{t=t_τ}^{t_{τ+1}} log π_θ(a_t | a_{<t})
```

### 2.2 Macro Action Termination Conditions

Four strategies are implemented. **Fixed n-gram is the default.**

**Strategy 1: Fixed n-gram**
- Group every n consecutive tokens into one macro action
- `|ωτ| = n` for all τ
- Default: n=5
- Last macro action may be shorter if sequence length is not divisible by n

**Strategy 2: Randomized n-gram**
- Predefined length list: `{2, 3, 5, 10}`
- Repeat this list 3 times → 12 elements
- Shuffle the list
- Apply lengths sequentially; if total doesn't cover sequence, append a large number (treat remainder as one macro action)
- Introduces variability across training steps

**Strategy 3: Parsing-based**
- Parse the generated response into a constituent tree (use `benepar` or `nltk` for NLP; use `tree-sitter` for code)
- DFS traversal of the tree
- Terminate a macro action when the current node has fewer than C=5 leaf tokens
- Single-token nodes are merged into the previous macro action (avoid punctuation-only macro actions)
- Fallback to standard PPO (n=1) when tokenizer mismatch occurs between generation tokenizer and parsing tokenizer

**Strategy 4: Perplexity-based**
- Compute per-token perplexity using the reference model's logits (no extra forward pass needed)
- `p_t = -log π_ref(a_t | a_{<t})`
- Build macro action by accumulating tokens while perplexity is monotonically decreasing
- Terminate when `ppl(ωτ ∪ a_{t_{τ+1}}) > ppl(ωτ)`

### 2.3 Value Function Estimation for Macro Actions

The macro action value is estimated from token-level values via a weighted sum:
```
V^π(sτ, ωτ) = Σ_{i=0}^{|ωτ|} σ_{t_τ+i} · V^π(s_{t_τ+i}, a_{t_τ+i})
```

Three σ assignment strategies (equal assignment is the default):

| Strategy | σ values | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Equal | `1/|ωτ|` for all tokens | Default in all experiments |
| Unit | `{0, 0, ..., 0, 1}` | Use last token's value only |
| Position-decayed | `1/((|ωτ|-i) · H)` where H is harmonic normalizer | Earlier tokens weighted less |

### 2.4 MA-PPO Objective

The clipped PPO objective at the macro action level:
```
L^MA-PPO(θ) = E_τ [ min(
    (π_θ(ωτ|sτ) / π_θ_old(ωτ|sτ)) · Â_τ,
    clip(π_θ(ωτ|sτ) / π_θ_old(ωτ|sτ), 1-ε, 1+ε) · Â_τ
)]
```

In practice, using log probabilities:
- `log_ratio_τ = Σ_{t∈ωτ} (log π_θ(a_t) - log π_θ_old(a_t))`
- `ratio_τ = exp(log_ratio_τ)`
- Apply clipping and advantage weighting per macro action
- Average the loss over all tokens (divide by total non-padding token count)

### 2.5 Advantage Estimation

Use Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) at the macro action level:
- Input: macro action values `V^π(sτ, ωτ)` and macro rewards `Rτ`
- GAE parameters: λ=0.95, γ=1.0 (from Table 5)
- The macro reward `Rτ` is the sum of token-level rewards within the macro action (ρ=1, so no discounting within a macro action)
- Token-level rewards consist of: KL penalty per token + final reward model score at the last token

### 2.6 Reward Shaping

Standard RLHF reward shaping applies:
```
R(x, y) = r_φ(x, y) - β · D_KL(π_θ(·|x) || π_sft(·|x))
```

The KL divergence is computed per-token:
```
kl_t = log π_θ(a_t | s_t) - log π_sft(a_t | s_t)
```

The RM score is placed at the final token; all other positions get only the KL penalty.

### 8.2 Core MA-PPO Functions to Implement

**Function 1: `get_macro_action_positions(start, mask, termination, **kwargs)`**

Returns a list of boundary indices `[start, b1, b2, ..., end]` where each consecutive pair defines one macro action.

```
Inputs:
  - start: index where the response begins (= prompt_length - 1)
  - mask: attention mask [1, seq_len]
  - termination: one of {'ngram', 'randomized_ngram', 'ppl', 'parser'}
  - n_gram: int (for ngram modes)
  - ppl: List[float] (for ppl mode)
  - cutoff: int (for parser mode, default C=5)

Output:
  - sequence: List[int] of boundary positions
```

**Function 2: `get_macro_action_values(values, mask, start, sequence)`**

Aggregates token-level values into macro action values using equal weighting (default).

```
Inputs:
  - values: tensor [1, seq_len] of token-level values from critic
  - mask: attention mask
  - start: response start index
  - sequence: boundary list from Function 1

Output:
  - inplace_values: tensor [1, num_macro_actions]
```

**Function 3: `policy_loss_macro_action(logprobs, old_logprobs, advantages, mask, sequence)`**

Computes the clipped PPO loss at macro action granularity.

```
Inputs:
  - logprobs: tensor [batch, seq_len] current policy log probs
  - old_logprobs: tensor [batch, seq_len] old policy log probs
  - advantages: tensor [batch, num_macro_actions]
  - mask: attention mask
  - sequence: boundary list

Output:
  - pg_loss: scalar
```

**Function 4: `critic_loss_macro_action(values, old_values, returns, mask, sequence)`**

Computes the value function loss at macro action granularity (clipped MSE).

**Function 5: `get_perplexity_sequence(logits, input_ids, start)`**

Computes per-token perplexity from reference model logits for PPL-based termination.

### 8.3 Key Integration Points in PPO Loop

The standard PPO loop needs these modifications:

```python
# After generating response and computing token-level values/rewards:

# 1. Compute macro action boundaries
sequence = get_macro_action_positions(start, action_mask, termination='ngram', n_gram=5)

# 2. Aggregate values and rewards to macro action level
macro_values = get_macro_action_values(old_values, action_mask, start, sequence)
macro_rewards = get_macro_action_values(old_rewards, action_mask, start, sequence)

# 3. Run GAE at macro action level (unchanged GAE algorithm, just on macro sequences)
advantages, returns = get_advantages_and_returns(macro_values, macro_rewards, gamma=1.0, lam=0.95)

# 4. Compute losses at macro action level
policy_loss = policy_loss_macro_action(logprobs, old_logprobs, advantages, action_mask, sequence)
critic_loss = critic_loss_macro_action(values, old_values, returns, action_mask, sequence)
```

## 11. Ambiguities and Open Questions

Several details are not fully specified in the paper:

1. **Macro action boundaries at batch level**: The paper shows single-sequence pseudocode. For batched training, each sequence in the batch will have different macro action boundaries. The loss must be computed per-sequence and then averaged, not batched naively.

2. **GAE implementation detail**: The paper says "apply GAE without modification." This means standard GAE runs on the macro action sequence `[V(s0), V(s1), ..., V(sT/n)]` with macro rewards `[R0, R1, ..., R_{T/n}]`. The resulting advantages are then broadcast back to all tokens within each macro action for the policy gradient computation.

3. **KL penalty aggregation**: The per-token KL penalties within a macro action need to be summed (not averaged) to form the macro reward `Rτ`, since the macro reward is defined as the sum of token-level rewards with ρ=1.

4. **Parsing tokenizer mismatch**: The paper mentions falling back to standard PPO when the parsing tokenizer and generation tokenizer disagree. The exact mismatch detection logic is not specified — a reasonable approach is to check if the total leaf count from the parse tree matches the token count from the generation tokenizer.

5. **Warmup steps for 7B**: Table 5 shows warmup steps=200 for 2B but the 7B column appears blank. Assume 200 as well unless evidence suggests otherwise.

6. **Critic loss clipping**: Standard PPO clips the value function update. The paper doesn't explicitly state whether this is used, but DeepSpeed-Chat includes it by default — keep it.

7. **WebGPT early stopping**: The paper mentions early stopping due to reward hacking on WebGPT. No specific stopping criterion is given — monitor for repetitive token generation and stop when detected.

8. **APPS unit test execution**: Requires a sandboxed execution environment. The paper doesn't specify timeout limits or memory constraints for code execution. A reasonable default is 3-second timeout per test case.

## Logic Analysis: trainers/ppo_experience_maker.py

# Logic Analysis: `trainers/ppo_experience_maker.py`

## Overview

`PPOExperienceMaker` is the rollout/data-collection component of the MA-PPO pipeline. It sits between the training loop and the model zoo, orchestrating a single forward pass through all four models (policy, reference, critic, reward) to produce a fully-annotated `Experience` object that the optimizer (`MAPPOTrainer`) can consume directly. No gradient computation happens here — this is pure inference.

The critical design constraint is that **macro action boundaries are computed per-sequence** (not per-batch), because different sequences have different lengths and different boundary positions. Everything downstream of `get_positions` must respect this per-sequence structure.

---

## 1. Data Structures

### 1.1 `Experience` Dataclass

The `Experience` object is the contract between `PPOExperienceMaker` and `MAPPOTrainer`. Every field must be populated before returning.

```
Experience:
    # Raw sequence data
    prompt_ids:       Tensor [batch, prompt_len]         — original prompt token ids
    response_ids:     Tensor [batch, response_len]       — generated response token ids
    full_ids:         Tensor [batch, prompt_len + response_len]  — concatenated
    attention_mask:   Tensor [batch, prompt_len + response_len]  — full sequence mask
    action_mask:      Tensor [batch, response_len]       — 1 for real response tokens, 0 for padding

    # Token-level quantities (shape: [batch, response_len])
    old_log_probs:    Tensor  — log π_θ(a_t | s_t) for each response token
    old_values:       Tensor  — V^π(s_t) from critic for each response token
    token_rewards:    Tensor  — shaped reward: KL penalty + RM score at last token

    # Scalar per sequence
    rm_score:         Tensor [batch]  — raw reward model output

    # Macro action structure (per-sequence, variable length)
    macro_sequences:  List[List[int]]  — boundary indices per sequence in batch
                                         length = batch_size, each inner list has
                                         len = num_macro_actions_i + 1

    # Macro-level quantities (padded to max_macro_actions in batch)
    macro_values:     Tensor [batch, max_macro_actions]  — aggregated critic values
    macro_rewards:    Tensor [batch, max_macro_actions]  — aggregated token rewards
    macro_mask:       Tensor [batch, max_macro_actions]  — 1 for real macro actions

    # GAE outputs (macro-level, same shape as macro_values)
    advantages:       Tensor [batch, max_macro_actions]
    returns:          Tensor [batch, max_macro_actions]
```

**Key design decision on padding**: Since each sequence has a different number of macro actions, `macro_values`, `macro_rewards`, `advantages`, and `returns` must be padded to `max_macro_actions` across the batch. A `macro_mask` tensor tracks which positions are real. This is needed so `MAPPOTrainer` can operate on batched tensors.

## 3. Step-by-Step Logic of `make_experience`

### Step 1: Generate Response

```python
response_ids, action_mask = policy.generate(
    input_ids=prompts,
    attention_mask=prompt_mask,
    max_new_tokens=config.ppo.max_response_len,
    temperature=config.ppo.temperature,
    top_p=config.ppo.top_p,
    top_k=config.ppo.top_k,
    do_sample=True
)
```

`policy.generate` returns:
- `response_ids`: shape `[batch, response_len]` — only the newly generated tokens
- `action_mask`: shape `[batch, response_len]` — 1 for real tokens, 0 for padding

**Important**: `response_len` may vary across calls due to early stopping (EOS token). The `action_mask` captures which positions are real response tokens vs. padding.

### Step 2: Construct Full Sequence

```python
full_ids = torch.cat([prompts, response_ids], dim=1)
# shape: [batch, prompt_len + response_len]

full_attention_mask = torch.cat([prompt_mask, action_mask], dim=1)
# shape: [batch, prompt_len + response_len]
```

The `start` index (boundary between prompt and response) is:
```python
start = prompts.size(1) - 1
```

This follows the paper's pseudocode convention: `start = prompts.size()[-1] - 1`. The response tokens occupy positions `[start+1, full_ids.size(1)-1]` in `full_ids`.

### Step 3: Compute Old Log Probabilities (Policy)

```python
# Under torch.no_grad() since this is experience collection
with torch.no_grad():
    policy_output = policy.forward(full_ids, full_attention_mask)
    policy_logits = policy_output.logits  # [batch, seq_len, vocab_size]
```

Then extract per-token log probs for response positions only:
```python
old_log_probs = _extract_log_probs(policy_logits, full_ids, action_mask, start)
# shape: [batch, response_len]
```

The `_extract_log_probs` helper:
1. Applies `log_softmax` over vocab dimension
2. Uses `gather` with `full_ids[:, start+1:]` as indices (shifted by 1 because logit at position `t` predicts token at position `t+1`)
3. Multiplies by `action_mask` to zero out padding positions
4. Returns shape `[batch, response_len]`

**Shift convention**: `log_prob[i, t]` = `log_softmax(logits[i, start+t])[full_ids[i, start+t+1]]`. This is the log probability of generating the `(t+1)`-th response token given all preceding context.

### Step 4: Compute Reference Log Probabilities

```python
with torch.no_grad():
    ref_output = ref_model.forward(full_ids, full_attention_mask)
    ref_logits = ref_output.logits  # [batch, seq_len, vocab_size]
    ref_log_probs = _extract_log_probs(ref_logits, full_ids, action_mask, start)
    # shape: [batch, response_len]
```

**Critical for PPL termination**: If `config.macro_action.termination == 'ppl'`, the `ref_logits` must be cached and passed to `macro_action.get_positions` in Step 8. Specifically, the per-token perplexity is:
```
p_t = -ref_log_probs[i, t]   (negative log prob = per-token perplexity contribution)
```

This reuses the already-computed `ref_logits` without an extra forward pass, as stated in the paper.

### Step 5: Compute Token-Level Values (Critic)

```python
with torch.no_grad():
    token_values_full = critic.get_values(full_ids, full_attention_mask)
    # shape: [batch, full_seq_len]

# Extract response portion only
token_values = token_values_full[:, start+1:]  # [batch, response_len]
token_values = token_values * action_mask       # zero out padding
```

The critic returns a value for every token position. We only need the response portion for GAE computation.

### Step 6: Compute Reward Model Score

```python
with torch.no_grad():
    rm_score = reward_model.compute_reward(full_ids, full_attention_mask)
    # shape: [batch]  — scalar per sequence
```

The reward model extracts the hidden state at the last non-padding token and passes it through the value head. This gives one scalar per sequence.

### Step 7: Compute Token-Level Rewards

```python
# KL penalty: per-token, shape [batch, response_len]
kl_penalty = reward_utils.compute_kl_penalty(
    policy_logprobs=old_log_probs,
    ref_logprobs=ref_log_probs,
    mask=action_mask
)
# kl_penalty[i, t] = old_log_probs[i, t] - ref_log_probs[i, t]
# Padding positions are zeroed by the mask

# Token rewards: KL penalty everywhere + RM score at last token
token_rewards = reward_utils.compute_token_rewards(
    rm_score=rm_score,
    kl_penalty=kl_penalty,
    mask=action_mask,
    kl_coeff=config.ppo.kl_coeff
)
# token_rewards[i, t] = -kl_coeff * kl_penalty[i, t]  for all t
# token_rewards[i, last_t] += rm_score[i]              at last real token
```

**Reward placement detail**: The RM score is added at the position of the last non-padding response token. Find this position using `action_mask`:
```python
last_token_idx = action_mask.sum(dim=1) - 1  # [batch] — 0-indexed within response
```

### Step 8: Compute Macro Action Boundaries (Per Sequence)

This is the most structurally complex step because it operates per-sequence.

```python
macro_sequences = []  # List[List[int]], one per sequence in batch

for i in range(batch_size):
    # Determine inputs for this sequence
    seq_action_mask = action_mask[i:i+1]  # [1, response_len]
    
    # For PPL termination: extract per-token perplexity for this sequence
    if config.macro_action.termination == 'ppl':
        seq_ref_logits = ref_logits[i:i+1, start:, :]  # [1, response_len+1, vocab]
        seq_input_ids = full_ids[i:i+1]
    else:
        seq_ref_logits = None
        seq_input_ids = None
    
    # For parser termination: get parse tree for this sequence
    if config.macro_action.termination == 'parser':
        response_text = tokenizer.decode(response_ids[i], skip_special_tokens=True)
        parse_tree = _get_parse_tree(response_text)
    else:
        parse_tree = None
    
    # Get boundaries
    sequence = macro_action.get_positions(
        start=start,
        mask=seq_action_mask,
        ref_logits=seq_ref_logits,
        input_ids=seq_input_ids,
        parse_tree=parse_tree
    )
    macro_sequences.append(sequence)
```

**`start` convention**: `start = prompts.size(1) - 1`. The `get_positions` method uses this as the first element of the returned boundary list. The response tokens are at positions `[start+1, ..., mask.size(1)-1]` in the full sequence indexing, but `get_positions` works with the `action_mask` which is already response-only. Clarify this with `MacroActionModule` — the `start` passed to `get_positions` should be `0` if `mask` is already the `action_mask` (response-only), or `prompts.size(1)-1` if `mask` is the full `attention_mask`. Based on the paper's pseudocode:
```python
start = prompts.size()[-1] - 1
action_mask = attention_mask[:, 1:]
sequence = get_macro_action_positions(start, action_mask, ...)
```
So `start` is in the coordinate system of `action_mask` (which is `attention_mask[:, 1:]`). The `action_mask` has the same length as `full_ids[:, 1:]`. The response tokens start at index `start` within `action_mask`.

### Step 9: Aggregate to Macro Action Level

For each sequence, aggregate token-level values and rewards to macro action level:

```python
all_macro_values = []   # List of tensors, variable length per sequence
all_macro_rewards = []

for i in range(batch_size):
    seq_token_values = token_values[i:i+1]   # [1, response_len]
    seq_token_rewards = token_rewards[i:i+1] # [1, response_len]
    seq_action_mask = action_mask[i:i+1]     # [1, response_len]
    
    # Aggregate values (equal-weighted mean within each macro action)
    mv = macro_action.get_values(
        token_values=seq_token_values,
        mask=seq_action_mask,
        start=start,
        sequence=macro_sequences[i]
    )
    # shape: [1, num_macro_actions_i]
    
    # Aggregate rewards (sum within each macro action, rho=1)
    mr = macro_action.get_rewards(
        token_rewards=seq_token_rewards,
        mask=seq_action_mask,
        start=start,
        sequence=macro_sequences[i]
    )
    # shape: [1, num_macro_actions_i]
    
    all_macro_values.append(mv.squeeze(0))   # [num_macro_actions_i]
    all_macro_rewards.append(mr.squeeze(0))  # [num_macro_actions_i]
```

**Reward aggregation vs. value aggregation**: `get_values` uses equal-weighted mean (σ = 1/|ω|) by default. `get_rewards` uses sum (ρ=1, so R_τ = Σ r_t within macro action). These are different operations and must not be confused.

### Step 10: Compute GAE at Macro Action Level

```python
all_advantages = []
all_returns = []

for i in range(batch_size):
    mv = all_macro_values[i].unsqueeze(0)   # [1, num_macro_actions_i]
    mr = all_macro_rewards[i].unsqueeze(0)  # [1, num_macro_actions_i]
    
    adv, ret = gae_utils.compute_advantages_and_returns(
        values=mv,
        rewards=mr,
        gamma=config.ppo.gae_gamma,   # 1.0
        lam=config.ppo.gae_lambda     # 0.95
    )
    # adv, ret: [1, num_macro_actions_i]
    
    all_advantages.append(adv.squeeze(0))  # [num_macro_actions_i]
    all_returns.append(ret.squeeze(0))     # [num_macro_actions_i]
```

**GAE with γ=1.0**: Since `gae_gamma=1.0` in all paper experiments, the GAE formula simplifies. The implementation in `gae_utils` must handle this without numerical issues (no exponential decay, just cumulative sums).

### Step 11: Pad and Package into Experience

Pad all variable-length macro action tensors to `max_macro_actions`:

```python
max_macro_actions = max(len(seq) - 1 for seq in macro_sequences)

macro_values_padded = torch.zeros(batch_size, max_macro_actions)
macro_rewards_padded = torch.zeros(batch_size, max_macro_actions)
advantages_padded = torch.zeros(batch_size, max_macro_actions)
returns_padded = torch.zeros(batch_size, max_macro_actions)
macro_mask = torch.zeros(batch_size, max_macro_actions)

for i in range(batch_size):
    n = len(macro_sequences[i]) - 1  # number of macro actions for sequence i
    macro_values_padded[i, :n] = all_macro_values[i]
    macro_rewards_padded[i, :n] = all_macro_rewards[i]
    advantages_padded[i, :n] = all_advantages[i]
    returns_padded[i, :n] = all_returns[i]
    macro_mask[i, :n] = 1.0
```

Then construct and return the `Experience` dataclass.

## 4. Private Helper Methods

### `_extract_log_probs(logits, full_ids, action_mask, start)`

Extracts per-token log probabilities for response tokens only.

Logic:
1. `log_probs_full = F.log_softmax(logits, dim=-1)`  — `[batch, seq_len, vocab]`
2. Response token ids are `full_ids[:, start+1:]`  — `[batch, response_len]`
3. `gathered = log_probs_full[:, start:-1, :].gather(2, full_ids[:, start+1:].unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1)`
   — `[batch, response_len]`
4. Apply `action_mask`: `gathered = gathered * action_mask`
5. Return `gathered`

The index arithmetic: `logits[:, start+t, :]` predicts the token at position `start+t+1` in `full_ids`. So `log_prob` for response token `t` (0-indexed) uses `logits[:, start+t, :]` and `full_ids[:, start+t+1]`.

### `_compute_kl_penalty(policy_logprobs, ref_logprobs, mask)`

Delegates to `reward_utils.compute_kl_penalty`. Included as a private method for clarity in `make_experience`.

### `_get_parse_tree(response_text)`

For parser-based termination only. Uses `benepar` for natural language or `tree-sitter` for code (based on `config.task`):
- If `config.task == 'apps'`: use `tree-sitter` Python grammar
- Otherwise: use `benepar` with `en_core_web_md` spaCy model

Returns the parse tree object, or `None` if parsing fails (triggers fallback to n=1 in `MacroActionModule._parser_positions`).

## 5. Key Invariants and Correctness Checks

### 5.1 n=1 Equivalence Check

When `config.macro_action.termination == 'ngram'` and `config.macro_action.n_gram == 1`:
- `macro_sequences[i]` has boundaries at every token position
- `macro_values[i]` equals `token_values[i]` (each macro action has one token, mean = that token's value)
- `macro_rewards[i]` equals `token_rewards[i]` (sum of one token = that token's reward)
- GAE on per-token values/rewards = standard token-level GAE
- `policy_loss` in `MAPPOTrainer` reduces to standard PPO loss

This is the key correctness check: n=1 must exactly reproduce vanilla PPO.

### 5.2 Reward Placement Verification

`token_rewards[i, t]` should be:
- `-kl_coeff * kl_penalty[i, t]` for all `t` where `action_mask[i, t] == 1`
- `rm_score[i] - kl_coeff * kl_penalty[i, last_t]` at the last real token `last_t`
- `0.0` for padding positions

### 5.3 Macro Reward Summation

`macro_rewards[i, τ]` = sum of `token_rewards[i, t]` for all `t` in macro action `τ`. Since `rho=1` (no intra-macro discounting), this is a simple sum. The RM score contribution appears in exactly one macro action (the one containing the last response token).

### 5.4 No Gradient Leakage

All operations in `make_experience` must be wrapped in `torch.no_grad()`. The `old_log_probs`, `old_values`, `token_rewards`, `advantages`, and `returns` stored in `Experience` are detached tensors used as targets/baselines during the optimization step. Gradients flow only through the fresh forward passes in `MAPPOTrainer.train_step`.

## 6. Memory and Efficiency Considerations

### 6.1 Reference Model Logits Caching

For PPL-based termination, `ref_logits` (shape `[batch, seq_len, vocab_size]`) must be retained after Step 4. For large vocabularies (Gemma has 256k tokens) and long sequences, this tensor can be very large. Consider:
- Only cache if `config.macro_action.termination == 'ppl'`
- Immediately delete after Step 8 to free memory
- For 27B models, this may require moving to CPU before caching

### 6.2 Per-Sequence Loop

The per-sequence loop in Steps 8-10 is a Python-level loop over `batch_size`. For `batch_size=256` (Gemma-2B PPO config), this loop runs 256 times per training step. Each iteration is lightweight (no GPU ops for ngram/randomized_ngram termination), but for parser-based termination, each iteration involves a CPU-side parse tree traversal. Profile this and consider parallelizing with `multiprocessing` if it becomes a bottleneck.

### 6.3 Detach Before Storing

Before packaging into `Experience`, detach all tensors from the computation graph:
```python
old_log_probs = old_log_probs.detach()
token_values = token_values.detach()
token_rewards = token_rewards.detach()
advantages_padded = advantages_padded.detach()
returns_padded = returns_padded.detach()
```

## 7. Edge Cases

### 7.1 Sequences Shorter Than n

If a response has fewer tokens than `n_gram`, the entire response becomes a single macro action. `get_positions` handles this by always appending the end boundary, so `macro_sequences[i] = [start, end]` and `num_macro_actions = 1`.

### 7.2 EOS Token Handling

When the policy generates an EOS token, subsequent positions in `response_ids` are padding. The `action_mask` correctly marks these as 0. The last real token (just before or at EOS) receives the RM score. The EOS token itself should not receive the RM score — use `action_mask.sum(dim=1) - 1` to find the last real token index, which excludes padding.

### 7.3 WebGPT Early Stopping

For `config.task == 'webgpt'`, monitor for reward hacking (repetitive token generation). A heuristic: if more than 30% of response tokens are repeated n-grams (n≥3), flag the sequence. This detection can be added as a post-generation check in `make_experience` before computing rewards.

### 7.4 Batch Size Mismatch After Generation

If some sequences in the batch hit `max_response_len` while others hit EOS earlier, `response_ids` will be padded to `max_response_len`. The `action_mask` handles this correctly. Ensure `full_ids` and `full_attention_mask` are consistently constructed.
